utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for D010-0728. In your binder, Mr. Vlajkovic, it is tab 17. Very well. Mr. Vlajkovic, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you comment on it, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an Official Note from a meeting with the Chief of the Supreme Command staff. It was held with the administration for the preparation of the republican organs for defence affairs. It is an administration of the federal defence ministry, that is to say, an institution which was outside the military system, and was not under the competence of the Supreme Command staff. It dealt with completely different issues as opposed to those that were dealt by the Chief of the Supreme Command staff. The contents of the Official Note, as well as the establishment position of that institution indicate that the document of the 3rd Army Command under resubordination of MUP units could not have been archived under number 2 alongside this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is this not the document which is actually under number 1 in the archive list, which we have seen as an exhibit? I believe the date indicated there was the 15th of May, 1999, and is it not the same document entered in the log-book under 248, also sub-item (1) dated the 15th of May, is it not the same document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I told you about that document, that in terms of its content as well as the origin, it's a document which could not have gone together with the 3rd Army Command document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Does it have to do anything with the rule on office management in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is completely contrary to the provisions of that rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes my direct examination of witness Mr. Vlajkovic. I wish to thank him for coming here to testify. Also, would I seek to tender this particular document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00607.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yesterday, during the course of your testimony you were shown several documents, and I want to go through some of them with you today, and I hope to get through them quite quickly. If we can start with D588, and this is a copy of the log-book of the cabinet of the Chief of Staff that is from your office. And if we could just simply have it displayed in the B/C/S in the full screen, just so we can have a close look at it. While this document is being brought up, sir, I have understood from testimony that this log-book was kept in your office; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was initially created and kept in our office, and we were supposed to retain it in the office for the next five to ten years.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, that only persons authorised to make entries in this log-book were the ones who actually made use of it, only persons from your office were authorised to do so, no?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is to say, the chief of office and the person, the clerk working there as well. These are the only two persons who were in charge of keeping this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So that would have been you and you also referred to a clerk?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I see you are shaking your head. Who were these two persons?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office within its composition has a separate sub-office, and the person working in that sub-office is the head of that office. He also has a clerk in charge of the log-book. So in other words, the head of the sub-office of the chief of office.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time it was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Go ahead. Yes, you were going to --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mr. Jankovic, Miodrag, warrant office.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So I take it, sir, from what you've said, other than these two persons, no one was authorised to make any entries in this log-book? Other officers weren't allowed to just come and make entries and log documents in this log-book?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person in charge and responsible for the log-book was the head of the sub-office. However, as the chief of office, I was entitled to make certain entries as well, because I was their superior office. In their absence, I could enter certain documents. That is why I had to be privy to the process itself. As far as the need for me to take part in it, that occurred when we organised our ourselves in shifts and when we worked around the clock, irrespective of whether an officer in charge was absent or present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. So I'm understanding these were all the persons who were authorised to log documents in this log-book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we can look at page 2 of this document. Yes. If we could just zoom in. I have a question, sir, regarding the right side of the document. It's column number 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: There are a number of names there, I see mostly your name, and I believe in some place there's also a Mr. Nikolic further down. What does that column represent, the one that has your names and then -- in column number 8, what is that for?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The column number 8 is something that is filled out by the log-book clerk, that is to say, the person who received documents. However, we can see that greatest number of documents were sent to me. The documents sent to Colonel Nikolic probably had to do with protocol obligations which he dealt with in the office, and for that reason it was sent to him. Colonel Nikolic, Dragutin Nikolic, he was the head of the protocol department of the General Staff. He was in charge of all protocol matters. And all such documents pertaining to that were sent directly to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the log-book clerk entered the name of the person to whom the document was sent. This is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. Now, sir, just directing your attention to entry -- the entry we are concerned with 248, we see there's a number 2 there, and you've spoken quite extensively on that. And if I could ask you if we could zoom out. Sorry. If we could have 248 on 247 together. One thing I notice sir, just looking at this document, and I am like yourself not a handwriting expert, is that entry number 2 of 248 and entry number 1 of 247 seem to have been done in the exact same handwriting, would you agree with that, sir, that the handwriting of both entries looks quite similar? These two documents seem to have been logged by the same person?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at the handwriting, most likely it was the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And both of these documents, the both of these entries say 3rd Army Command, no, that's what is written there?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can zoom out again. Sorry, we are zooming in and out of this document. We see that both of these documents, the one in the first line of 247 and the one in the second line of 248 are logged as being received by you; correct? That's what column 8 says, has your name Vlajkovic next to it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, would you allow for the possibility that this matter which concerns us here about this mysterious entry number 2 under 248, that this was simply a mistake made by the person who was entering the information in this log-book and that instead of logging it under 247 it was logged by error under 248 with an unrelated document? Do you allow for that possibility, sir, that that's what happened here?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is always a possibility of making a mistake, but if there had been a mistake there, it should have been a correction too. If we suppose that this indeed was a mistake, it should have been corrected subsequently. However, it is my view that the log-book clerk would not have made such a type of error.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But mistakes were made from time to time, no, in entering documents in the log-book?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And it could have happened that the person entering the log-book at the time did not realise this was a mistake so no correction was made subsequently, correct, that is also possibility of what could have happened, why there's no correction?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said already, mistakes are possible, but the nature of this document required greater attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would rather suppose that this was not a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. But this is just something you are supposing? You do accept that mistakes are possible when logging documents?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could go now to D584. This is the archive list. We only need the B/C/S version. If that could be displayed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If I understand, sir, this is the list that was prepared in August of 1998 when -- in 1999, I'm sorry, for the hand-over of these documents to the military archive?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we see the date on this is 10th August, 1999, that would have been when the hand-over occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that date the archive list was created and the archive documents gathered and handed over to the military archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. And before this list was sent to the archive, can I take it that you as head of this office would have looked at it and approved it? You would have checked the list? Or was there someone else responsible for doing it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I testified yesterday, in August I was already preparing myself to leave to a new position. The dead-line for this task was the end of the year, and I delegated that responsibility to my deputy, Colonel Milan Radoicic, who at the same time was preparing himself to assume the duties of the chief of office. I authorised him to complete this task in technical terms. He was the person tasked with completing the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I take it, sir, this was not the first time you were doing a hand-over of documents to the military archive? This was quite regular procedure, that you at a certain point would hand over documents that you had in your office to the military archive for a more permanent archiving?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the office we used to hand over archival material once a year. However, these were war-time documents, and the chief had ordered that the archival process of all war-time documentation be completed and that all documents be handed over to the military archives. Peacetime documents were dealt with slightly differently, i.e., we usually handed them over in bulk at the beginning of each year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. I see that. I see this is a typed-up document, so I take it, sir, that once this document was typed up, you didn't make any corrections to it? Your office didn't make any handwritten corrections to it? You would hand in a clean typed-up list to the archive?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We needed to hand over a list with all the columns filled in to the military archives. Once we had processed such documents, those working in the military archives would process them further in order. We can see that our archive on the 24th of September, in other words, it was handed over in August, but the archives have only processed it in late September. We handed over the form with no corrections whatsoever. Perhaps we should focus on column number 3, if I may, where one is supposed to answer the contents, a note on the contents of the document. The person in charge of the log-book would enter such a remark. We will need that later, I presume. Or do you want me to go on?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, that goes well beyond my question actually, sir. I think that is sufficient for now. Just drawing your attention to the, let's say it's column 4 from what I can see, it's at the bottom of the page, we see there's a handwritten annotation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we can zoom in maybe we can see it better.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The number 217-1 has been entered. This would have been -- from what I understand, this would have been something that the archivist at the military archive would have written on the document. It wasn't made by you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This was after further review of your list, and they would have inserted this correction here? After they had analysed the documents in more detail that you sent them?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person reviewing the archival material did so following the list. Under number 6, that person ascertained that the number of the document was incorrect and made corresponding corrections. There might have been an attached document, the number of which had not originally been entered, and that is why we have this additional entry. That would have been the procedure followed by the military archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we see number -- page 2 of this -- the next page of this document. I'm sorry, I believe it's page 3. If we can zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We see here, sir, that there are quite a few of additional corrections that are made, right, handwritten corrections?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And these would have also been mistakes that had been spotted by the archive officer in charge of doing the review of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm not going to take you through the whole archive list, sir, but just reviewing it for the purpose of your testimony, I notice that it is, in fact, quite full of corrections, documents that were omitted, incorrect reference number, incorrect page numbers. You agree with me that there -- we just see it on this page, there are quite a number of corrections that have been entered?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And these would have been all corrections to the mistakes that had been made in this the log-book that your office was keeping; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we can just move onto the next document. This is a document you've spoken about extensively. This D585. It's a document we are concerned with here, it's a document prepared by General Pavkovic dated 25th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm sure you remember this document, you've been shown it now several times both here and in your previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could just see the second page. We only need -- well, we can have both of them up. If we can see the second page of this document. And in the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So I understand from your testimony yesterday, sir, that on this second page --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, we can zoom out, please, in the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: On this second page you recognise this stamp from your office? This document bears a stamp?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And it is marked as being received on the 26th of May of 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And, sir, you strike me, just from having heard your testimony here today, as someone who takes his job quite seriously, so I take it, sir, that the stamp that your office had to stamp documents upon receipt, that wasn't something that just anyone -- any other officer could just come in and use, correct? Only authorised people from your office had access to this stamp?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I commented on these two documents yesterday. And because of other technical indicators when you compare them --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, if I just stop you there. We have your testimony, and I'm quite clear on your position on this document and the other unstamped documents so there no need for you to repeat that. All I'm asking you is did anyone else other than the persons authorised in your office have access to the stamp that you use to stamp documents when they were received by the cabinet of the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ, or was it just persons in your office who had access to that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only authorised persons that I referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So this stamp could not have been put by anyone other than persons authorised to stamp documents when they were received; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, yesterday in response to when you were explaining your position on this document and the other version we've seen, which does not bear the stamp, you said something that just made me quite curious. You were explaining your position and you said: "The significance of the document and the person it was addressed to would not mean that it would be archived with only five or six numbers." Now, sir, I'm quite curious to know, who told you that this was a significant document? Why did you say that yesterday when you were referring to this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, preparing for this trial I informed myself, I looked over this document, but that includes also my testimony in the Milutinovic case, and this is why I said it was an important document. I looked at the contents while preparing for my testimony. With contents like this, I would probably be able to reconstruct things and recall whether it had reached the office or not, so in that context, I said that the contents were important. But I learned the contents while I was preparing for my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But, sir, I'm sure that the Chief of the General Staff received many important documents during the course of his work, no?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear why you say -- you have noted this document as being a document significant importance. Is that something someone told you about the document, that this was a document of significance?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is my own assessment. Resubordination of the MUP forces or placing of all the forces in the zone of operations under a single command is a document that is not unimportant. That is why I said that the contents are important. This is not something to be underestimated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, yesterday you were shown by my learned colleague this document, and it was compared with the unstamped version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Maybe we could have the other version up. This is P888.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You remember that both documents were shown to you together? They were put up on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could have the second page of the other document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, when you were being shown these two documents one of the things my learned colleague drew your attention to was the signature under where it says commandant or commander, and he said -- where we can see the signature and the stamp so that we can see them more closely, and your answer -- you said: "I am not a handwriting analysis expert, but it's evident here that it's not the signature and the stamp is different, indicating that it's a different copy." So you commented that these two documents had a different signature? Do you recall that testimony yesterday? This is at page 11220 of yesterday's transcript. Do you recall saying that, sir, making that comment?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do recall it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, you told us yesterday and you told my learned colleague in response to one of his questions that you recall testifying in the Milutinovic trial and that you would not change the answers that you had given in that trial? Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I take it, sir, that in that trial you told the truth? You recall under oath?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was expecting a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That was my question, sir. Thank you for that answer. Now, I just wanted to direct your attention to a passage of that transcript. This is page 16048. This is page 28 in e-court of the transcript. And this is a passage where you are being shown both of these documents, and in response to a question from Judge Bonomy regarding the stamped version, you say -- and this as the witness: "If I understood your question correctly, the signature is that of the commander, but what is visible here -- I beg your pardon, that both copies were signed by the commander, General Nebojsa Pavkovic." Do you recall giving that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember saying that, but I'm not asserting that this was not signed by the commander. Both signatures are the signatures of the commander, but obviously this is not a copy or these are not copies of the same documents. The copies are different, so as far as I'm concerned, these are two separate documents. This is Nebojsa Pavkovic's signature, but it's not the same on both copies. If it's an identical copy there can be no difference. According to the rules, the chief would sign one document which would then be copied and distributed. He would sign the first copy, the original. This is what I was talking about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. So we can agree that both of these documents bear the signature of General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we just focus on the one that does not bear the stamp of your office as having been received on the 26th of May, would you accept the possibility, sir, that that copy of the document is simply a copy that was received by this court, and it's a copy that -- of the document before it was received or before it was sent out to your office? Could you accept that possibility that this is simply a copy of the document before it was received by your office?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I try to understand your question and place that in the context of how this is regulated by the rules, I really don't know how to answer. The commander did sign one copy which was distributed, archived, or dispatched. All the rest are copies which would need to be the same according to all the other technical elements. I don't know if he signed anything later and what that was, but pursuant to the rules, he would sign one document which then -- which would then be copied and distributed. So the copies that are made from that one document cannot be different from the original. All the copies made later must be identical to the original and the copy itself must be certified. So you would certify the copy, but then that copy would have an original stamp. This is how it should be done by the rules. But here this does not seem to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But you've looked at both documents and they have the same contents, correct? I mean, you've studied these documents in quite some detail to prepare for your testimony? The contents is the same?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So it is possible, sir, that the document we see on the left is not a certified copy, it's just simply a copy of the document before it was sent out, that this court received. Is that possible, sir, do you accept that possibility that that's what this is?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say whether that can be the case or not, but what I'm saying is that the document that a person would sign is treated pursuant to the rules. It's distributed. What the copies are before signing, after signing, before dispatch, after dispatch, it's very hard for me to say. As far as I'm concerned here, it's the same document, this is a fact, signed by the commander, but the signatures on the two documents are different. If it were a copy, then the two documents should be identical, there should be no differences. If I understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that, sir. We'll move on from this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If I could have P1240 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is also a document that was shown to you yesterday. Do you recall looking at this document? This was a document prepared by the Pristina Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I take it you've also had the time to look and study this document in preparation for your testimony here; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did look at the contents of the document, but not really in detail. I know roughly what it's about. But I can see that it's a document of the Pristina Corps sent to the 3rd Army commander, meaning that the document was not available to me and could not have been available to me before I began to prepare for my testimony here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I know, sir, I'm not suggesting it was at all. Now, sir, having studied this document, you probably noticed that they refer to the same topics, correct? I mean, this one and the previous one we looked at that was prepared by General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And yesterday when you were being shown this document, one of the things you noticed was that this document did not have a distribution list? You mentioned that as one of the problems you saw with the document. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes. This is just a technical problem, a technical failing of the document. In principle, the document is addressed to the 3rd Army commander personally, but it can also be dispatched to some other people at the same time which would then be noted at the end of the document. And because this is a strictly confidential document, the number of the copy would also be indicated and so this -- because this was an archived document, it should be copy number 2 if it's sent to this particular person, and that should be evident from the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But, sir, if General Lazarevic, who wrote this document, only intended for this document to reach General Pavkovic, the commander of the 3rd Army, he did not need to include any distribution list, no? I mean, that wouldn't be required if that was the only person he wanted to send this document to?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the document is being addressed and sent to only one person, that does not rule out the need for the document to be archived. And then you would need to note that copy number 1 was sent to the archives, and copy number 2 was sent to the addressee.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But, sir, you are not really familiar with the practices used by the Pristina Corps when logging and archiving their documents; correct? I mean, you did not work there. I know there are general practices but you were not working there at the time, so.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm talking from the aspect of the rules regulating these matters and applied in the Army of Yugoslavia throughout.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So the fact that this document did not indicate the number of copies made could have just been simply an omission, correct, when it was prepared?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could consider it an omission, but you could also consider it a violation of the rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. And if General Lazarevic just intended for General Pavkovic to receive it who worked in the same office and simply handed it himself or sent one of his officers to hand it over personally, there would be no need for any sort of distribution list?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of the way the document was distributed, it still had to be archived and logged in, which this document does indicate in the upper left-hand corner. It was -- it went through the office, it was logged in the log-book, verified with a stamp and then handed over to the army commander. If they worked in the office together, well, then, I don't know. There is no stamp there and no log-book. This should have been done or must have been done through the person responsible for such duties. It had to be done through the logging office.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. But I understand your position that what you are saying is that procedure wasn't followed in this case. That is your objection with the document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is one of the things that I'm noting in relation to this document. I don't know how significant that is for the proceedings. But technically, this was not processed in accordance with the rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I see that, sir. I want to move on to a different topic that you spoke about yesterday. And we are no longer going to be looking at the document on the screen. Yesterday at the beginning of your testimony, you spoke about the evening briefings that were held at the VJ General Staff. Do you remember talking about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Evening briefings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And I understood your testimony to be that you regularly attended these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And once the conflict started, the NATO bombing complaints started in March of 1999, did these meetings happen on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day, but I can also note that the Chief of Supreme Command staff did not preside over each of the evening briefings. In his absence these were chaired by either his deputy or the chief of the operations administration. But the briefings were held practically every day until the end of the bombing campaign.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when circumstances required, were there also morning briefings held at the VJ General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part there were afternoon briefings. I cannot recall any morning briefings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. You don't recall that in the mornings there were sometimes as well when required meetings that took place?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. They could have been held later because the usual time was between 17- and 1800 hours. Sometimes it would happen that because of some duties, it would be held at 2000 hours. But I don't recall any morning briefings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. And you said yesterday, if I recall your testimony correctly, that these meetings were attended by General Ojdanic, and you said by his deputy sometimes. And also by the heads of sectors and administrations of the VJ General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if I understood your evidence correctly, the purpose of these meetings was to go over events that had taken place the previous day?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was there generally a format followed? I mean, were these meetings usually opened by General Ojdanic or his deputy who was there in his place, whenever general Ojdanic was absent, was that usually the form that he would open the meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The usual minutes were not done --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The usual agenda were not usually done. The meeting would usually be opened by his chief or his deputy depending who was conducting the session. Then the first address would be by the chief of the operations team that monitored the situation 24 hours a day. Then after his report the other members would then make their own assessments and evaluations and possible suggestions according to a set order, which would probably be first the person General Krga with the foreign affairs estimate of the situation and then there would be others who followed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. I see. And you have explained in your statement and also you said yesterday in your testimony that there was no official record kept of these meetings? These weren't tape recorded and later there was an official transcript prepared, correct, that wasn't done?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were no technical possibilities for recordings, but the minutes were kept regularly in a book, and this was in the hands of the operations administration, and this was most frequently done by Colonel Paskas and Colonel Mucibabic [Realtime translation read in error "Vuci Babic"] from that administration. They would be writing the notes from the briefing into the book. They are not stenographers, so they would note down whatever they managed to note down and what they thought was important using, as far as I could see and as far as I could know, some abbreviations of their own in order to be able to note down as much as possible. I'm saying that because now we are having problems to decipher those abbreviations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. So these two persons, Colonel Mucibabic and Paskas -- I think Mucibabic, his name is incorrect in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: These would be the two persons taking handwritten notes during the course of these meetings. Now, I believe you told us yesterday that at the conclusion of these meetings General Ojdanic would issue tasks to those present?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of the Supreme Command staff issued assignments also during the briefings which was something that I did note down. At the end he could repeat that also and issue new assignments. During the briefing he would immediately order that this, this, and that, had to be done or taken care of, and at the end of the meeting, he would summarise all of that including those same tasks and perhaps others, maybe some assignments that did not directly arise from the things that were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And these tasks once they were issued, in order for them to be carried out, they would have to be written up somehow, I believe, and sent to the respective administrations that were to carry out these tasks?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of my own notes and having followed the briefings and the things that the chief and the others stated and commented on, after the chief would complete the briefing, I would then formulate the conclusions and the assignments. I would put them in proper language. I would type it up, copy, and dispatch that to all of those who were indicated as responsible for each assignment. So the person responsible for an assignment would have by midnight a typed updated list of assignments and was obliged to refer back to me, report back to me about the implementation of those assignments. On the basis of those reports back to me and monitoring the activities that the Supreme Command staff at the following briefing, I would then inform the Chief of the Supreme Command staff or the entire Supreme Command present at the briefing whether the tasks were implemented and what stage of the implementation they were in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So I understand that it would be you, the person doing the follow-up of whether these tasks were actually being implemented, the tasks that were should at these evening briefings by General Ojdanic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, yesterday during your testimony you were shown Exhibit D606.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could have that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 7th of April. Do you remember seeing this document yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in connection with this document yesterday, you said that this is probably a transcript of the minutes from a briefing and you said the minutes were kept in an A4 copy book and somebody transcribes these, and you went on later and this is page 11213 to say: "We can't see any authorisation of this transcript. There's no indication that it's been verified." And you say, "... certain imprecisions that combined with the lack of any data about verification make it difficult to determine how authentic it is." Do you recall saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said, and I stand by it. I am sure, though, that this was not a shorthand note, but that this was a transcript. The people who took notes were not stenographers. They took notes as much as they were be able to do. And I also said this is a transcript of these evening briefings and it was done and it was really pregnant with many imprecisions. There was no authorisation or certification, and as such, this transcript I don't know in what way and to what extent it can serve as evidence material, given that it hasn't been authorised. That it's imprecise, that it contains so many imprecisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, we can look at another document, and this is a similar document you were shown yesterday, and this is D008-2190. This is a document dated 7th of April. Do you recall being shown this document yesterday, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to look at the date. The 7th of April, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in connection with this document, you said at page 11214, it's again a transcript from the book of minutes kept at the briefings of the Supreme Command staff, and this one is of 7th of April and you said: "It has the same features ... unauthorised with many imprecisions that make it difficult to interpret it." Do you recall saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the note-takers used certain abbreviations that were not in standard use. For that reason it would have been better for this transcript to have been authorised, which will enable the author to know exactly what he meant, and that would contribute to its being more precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall, sir, that you were shown this same document in the Milutinovic case, and in that case it was 3D639? And this is testimony that starts at page 16036. At this time you were shown this document by counsel for the Ojdanic Defence. I'm just going to read to you very briefly what you said in connection with this document. You say -- you were asked: "Q. Sir, you went to these evening briefings during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you present at all of them, at most of them?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down when reading. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: "Were you present at all of them, at most of them?" And this is on page 16037 I'm reading. And you said: "I could say that I was present at a large part of them." And you were asked about a passage in this document, and this is on page 3, which says: "Review of sentences to read inside and to keep a diary of assignments." In connection with this passage, you said: "There was a discussion over the previous days or in previous speeches," and this is on page 16038, "about the members of the army who had been processed for war crimes and committed crimes and to inform the units and the public in more detail about this." So you said: "So what I said was not really recorded quite correctly, but my proposal had to do with having the information about the perpetrators of crimes announced to the units, the members of the units, where these crimes were committed." Do you recall saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember saying that have to interpret this transcript as to what I could of said at that moment, and this is in support of the validity of these transcripts. Later on I tried to reconstruct what it was I could have been talking about. However, since there was discussion to have full names or maybe family member names in the public media of the people who were brought to trial, and if I mentioned crimes in that contents, one of the crimes was also desertion or failure to respond to a call-up, or evasion to serve in the reserve forces. So in that sense, I said, I probably said that if that was the case, that shouldn't be published in the media but in conformity with military rules, this should have been announced in front of the unit where these crimes took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. But you would agree with me, sir, that when this same document was shown to you by Ojdanic Defence, you said nothing about the fact that you had concerns regarding its authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't ask me about authenticity, but basically what I said was that that was a transcript of the minutes, but since it was I who said that, I later recalled what I said in principle which I couldn't be able to say about someone else who stated similar things. It is true, I didn't tackle the issue of validity, but I told you essentially what this was all about, what kind of documents we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So we can agree that you confirmed that you were at that meeting and that you made a statement there although it might not have been recorded exactly in the same terms as how you stated it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you allow me, I interpreted my own words. But as for the statements made by other persons, I wouldn't be able to do that. In other words, by providing authorisation for this transcript, it could become much better and then we can discuss what was being debated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender this exhibit. I'm going to move to a different one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01531.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you were also shown in the course of the Milutinovic case, exhibit, which in this case is 65 ter 04021, if we could have that up on the screen. If that case that was 3D580. And I'm referring to a passage that is at page 16088, begins there which is page 74 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in relation to this document, which is dated 26th of March, 1999, Judge Bonomy asked you a question and he said: "If we could go back to the question you asked, is the format of the minutes of the briefing that you're familiar with -- is this the format of the minutes of the briefing that you're familiar with?" And you said: "No, no, this format is something that I saw during my preparation for my testimony and --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: My apologies again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And it's an excerpt from the minutes from the original book where the actual minutes were taken by hand, and then you were asked by counsel for the Prosecution Mr. Stamp: "When you say excerpt, what do you mean?" And you say: "Not excerpt, but typed as written in the actual minutes." Do you recall saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in detail, but this is minutes of the meeting that has been retyped or a transcript thereof made, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, can we agree on something that these different documents that we've been looking at are not an official record of what was said at these meetings? These are not like the VJ collegium minutes where an official tape-recorded record was kept and then that was typed up?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Handwriting notes were transcribed, but there we have a tape recording transcribed, and there's a difference between the two. Here we have the transcript of handwritten notes taken during the very meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And can we also agree, sir, that what the documents we've been looking at that refer to these collegium briefings that took place in once the conflict had started, these are a typed-up version of the handwritten minutes that were taken? That's what you've previously stated, no, that they are a typed-up version of the notes that were taken? I'm leaving aside the issue of whether there were imprecisions and corrections.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And so if I understand your answer correctly, this would have been a typed-up copy of the notes taken either by Colonel Mucibabic or Colonel Spasic [as interpreted] who you have told us were the ones taking notes at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Paskas, not Spasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misspoke. So it's Colonel Mucibabic or Colonel Paskas. That's what this would be, yes. Thank you. Now, sir, you've told us that you regularly attended these meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this week we had the -- your deputy Mr. Radoicic testify here, and he told us that only once or twice you were prevented from attending -- from personally being there, would that be accurate? That you were there mostly throughout when these meetings occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said is that I attended a great majority of the meetings. Probably Colonel Radoicic concluded that I missed one or two meetings and it might as well be true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. That's fair enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could I have this document exhibited before I move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before we do, the documents on the screen do not appear the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I thought we had corrected the translation of this document. There might be a problem with the English translation, Your Honour. I can look into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a different document, if you look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know. What I'm saying is I think we may have uploaded an incorrect translation in e-court. So at this stage if we could have this marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01532 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I note, Your Honour, that this is the copy that was shown to the witness in the Milutinovic case, and if we scroll down on the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are speaking of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The Serbian, yes. If we scroll down on the B/C/S version of the document, I don't see it, but this in any case was Exhibit 3D580 in that case. I just say that for clarity of the record, Your Honour. I want to move away from this document, if we could have D006-3266 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is a document -- these are again these typed-up minutes of the evening briefings, and this one is dated 3rd of April, 1999, and we see, if we look at the document, different persons speak on the first page, and the last one to speak in both the English and B/C/S is Colonel Gajic. Do you recall what was his position at the time? We are talking in April 1998. Do you recall what Colonel Gajic's position was, what rank he held?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember at the time he was a colonel, and he was the head of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now if we can turn to page 2 both in the English and the B/C/S, I'm going to read out a passage of what has been recorded in these notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is still Mr. Gajic -- Colonel Gajic speaking. It says: "With regard to the territory there are problems with paramilitary formations. Intelligence has it that there are volunteers who have arrived in KLM without the army being aware of it, and these are the MUP reserve forces," -- and then there's a proposal -- "inform MUP and other organs to undertake measures within their competence."

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we can also now turn to page 4 both in the English and in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I just want to read out another passage to you before I ask you but this. So it's at the bottom in the B/C/S, I'm looking at number 9, and this is General Ojdanic speaking and he says: "For military formations documents in keeping with the Federal Republic and Ministries of the Interior." Now, sir, do you recall the issue of paramilitary formations being raised at this meeting, paramilitary formations that were attached to the MUP as reserve forces? Do you recall this issue being discussed by General Gajic and -- Colonel Gajic and General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of paramilitary formations that should have been placed under the army control is something that I do remember about it. It is difficult for me, though, to tell you the dates. It was being discussed but most often within the context of an obligation and even orders issued by the Chief of General Staff, that under the law, these paramilitary formations be placed under the army control. I know nothing about MUP paramilitary formations. We didn't discuss this kind of units, and we didn't seek any solution of how to treat them. But there was an order of the Chief of General Staff for paramilitary formations or volunteers who refused to be placed under the army control to be disarmed and removed from combat operations. Those were the orders issued but how it was implemented in practice, I don't know much about. Speaking about MUP paramilitary formations, I don't know how they acted and treated these units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not asking if you know how the MUP acted or treated these units, I was just asking about what is being said here. Now, this number 9 I just read, which is headed "paramilitary formations" is noted at the end of these briefing notes, and it's General Ojdanic speaking and you have already told us that at the end of these briefing notes he would generally issue tasks to those present. Do you remember you've just told us that earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You've told us also that you were the one in charge of following up and making sure that these tasks were carried out, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, my question, sir, is where it says here, "Document in keeping with the Federal and Republic Ministries of Interior," who would be the addressee of this task, who would be in charge of documenting this or of contacting the MUP about these -- this information that is being given at this briefing about the existence of paramilitary formations attached to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the structure and tasks of the Supreme Command staff, this task was to be carried out by the head of the security administration. His duty was to draft a document to be sent to the republic MUP containing the observations that we made and that would be verified by the chief and the chief -- or the head of the administration would then forward this document. Having forwarded this document by the head, I would have deemed this task to be carried out. If you look at the list of assignments from this particular briefing, probably you can find who was appointed to carry out this task and what the dead-lines were. But basically this was under the jurisdiction of the head of the security administration, and I think it was Colonel Gajic who was at the helm of this administration at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know to whom in the MUP he would send this document that you spoke about containing the observations that were made during this briefing? Who would this be addressed to in the republican MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to a particular person, but normally that would be sent to the office of the minister of the interior, because the system of communication with institutions outside the military such as ministries, the federal government, the president of the FRY, and other dignitaries, all the communications normally went through their respective offices. They were delivered to the offices or directly to the responsible minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And the minister of interior at the time was Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if we look at number 2, which is on the page, and it's also under the tasks that are issued but General Ojdanic, and we have that also in the English on the top of the page, it says "prepare denials on refugees" and the -- in parentheses, we have "administration for information." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, if how we should be reading these minute, this would be a task that had been issued to the administration for information to prepare denials on refugees?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move on from this document. Your Honours, at this stage I seek to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01533.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now I would like to have another document up, and this is dated -- it's document 65 ter 04025.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I just want to draw your attention to page 1 both in the English and B/C/S, and these are again briefing notes of the Supreme Command dated -- Supreme Command Chief of Staff, and they are dated 16th of April, 1999. And if we see number 3 we have again Colonel Gajic speaking, and the third bullet point under his name indicates: "I propose political measures be taken, there are problems with paramilitary activities." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to page 4 in both versions of the document. If we look at number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It says, "security administration" -- I see the document is being enlarged there. Thank you. "Security administration - investigate and prove the existence of paramilitary activities, place, purpose, who and by whose approval they entered the territory of KiM." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So, sir, I take it that -- and this, I should have clarified, is again under the section of "Tasks and Responsibilities," and they are issued by General Ojdanic. So I take it, sir, that based on what you've told us, we see here that the security administration is again being tasked to investigate and approve the existence of paramilitary activities in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just for clarification, if we can scroll up on both versions of the document. We see there where it says, "Tasks and Responsibilities," it says NSVK; you see that? I'm probably not --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it stands for the Supreme Command Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So that would be a reference, an abbreviation for General Ojdanic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that be Exhibit P01534.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to move on to a different document, so I suggest we have the break two minutes early so I don't have to interrupt my questions on the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could now have D008-1936 up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And, sir, while this document is being brought up is again a set of briefing notes, and it's dated 22nd of April, 1999. I'm just waiting, sir, for the document to come up in the English on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to page 4 both on the English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I would like to draw your attention to number 3 on that page. This is again, sir, this is the conclusion of these minutes, and this is General Ojdanic who is speaking. Now, number 3 there, one of the tasks he is issuing, says "Contact the state security or DB and the minister of interior regarding volunteers." You see that number 3 up on the screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, earlier when we had seen another one of these notes where General Ojdanic was issuing similar instructions, you had told us that the person responsible for carrying out this task would normally have been the head of security administration Colonel Gajic. Now, would he also have been the person responsible for carrying out this task that he is issuing here, the contact say security and the minister of interior regarding volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01535.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And finally, sir, if we could have up on the screen, D008-2144. And these are briefing notes of the Chief of Staff of the VJ General Staff of 6 May 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we could have page 3 both in the English and the B/C/S. If we could scroll down on the B/C/S and in the English zoom in somewhere on the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we see the abbreviation that you have told us stands for the chief of the VJ General Staff or General Ojdanic, and it says: "Closing speech and task," and under there there's a number 1: "Are there any paramilitary units in Kosovo and Metohija?" And Colonel Gajic says: "Yes, there are unfortunately." Do you see that passage there?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And based on what you've told us about the discussions on paramilitary units at these briefings, can we conclude that this is yet another occasion when the issue of paramilitary units is brought up at these briefing sessions that were carried out?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If I could tender this exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01536.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, moving away from these briefing notes, I would like to show you a press article, and this is 01696. And this is a press article which is headed "Army, police heads inform Milosevic of successful defence." And if we could zoom in a bit more on the document. Thank you. Now, sir, this press article reports on a meeting that took place and the 4th of May and among those listed here as having attending are President Milosevic; 3rd Army commander, Nebojsa Pavkovic; General Sreten Lukic, and there are other persons mentioned including General Ojdanic. If -- I'm sorry, I have a bit of a cold so I'm losing my voice -- we could scroll down to a bit to the bottom sentence starting with "along with carrying out tasks." So here we see that what is being reported it says, "along with carrying out these complex tasks, these security forces dealt with numerous cases of violence, killings, pillage, and other crimes arresting several hundred perpetrators whose crimes were a great danger to the civilian population." This I put to you, sir, is an article that refers to this situation in Kosovo at the time. Now, sir, do you first recall General Ojdanic attending a meeting on the 4th of May with the persons that I have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard for the first time about the meeting discussed here when I was shown these documents. The chief did have meetings with the supreme commander, and there were sessions of the Supreme Defence Council. As for who attended those sessions and in what capacity, that is something I was not privy to. However, as for the meetings attended by the chief of staff, there must have been at least minimum preparations for each and every one of them. Documents were supposed to be read, things prepared, et cetera. I don't know about this meeting in particular, whether it was held indeed, and whether it was held on that date. It seems a bit odd to me that the supreme commander is holding a meeting and being briefed by Ojdanic and Lukic and also in attendance were their superiors. I didn't follow the press at that time because I could not, therefore, I don't recall having seen this article at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I put to you, sir, that this was published in "Politika" magazine. Are you familiar with that publication?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of the publication. And I was also able to read it, but not during the bombing campaign. There was simply no time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. It was probably a very busy time for you. Sir, you said that there were usually preparations made, minimum preparations for each and every meeting. You don't recall having done any preparation for this specific meeting on the 4th of May which this article reports General Ojdanic attended?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, I'll try to be more precise. I wanted to say at least minimum preparations. If some meetings were held at short notice. I don't recall though, having prepared any materials for the chief where he would have briefed on the issues reported by "Politika."

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And, sir, just to clarify, I did not suggest that he was doing a briefing, that's not what the article said. The briefings were made by General Pavkovic and General Lukic. So I did not suggest to you that it was General Ojdanic who was briefing, simply that he was present at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the system of command, the Supreme Commander can only be briefed by the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, or, if he authorised the 3rd Army commander to do so. That is based on the system of command. If this was conveyed by "Politika" correctly, then the system of command must have been incorrectly applied. Therefore, I question some of the allegations in this article. I don't recall a meeting at which the Chief of the Supreme Command staff was accompanied by the 3rd Army commander when he had to deal with certain issues with President Milosevic. That would have been against all existing regulation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. So I understand your evidence is that you don't recall this specific meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just for reference, Your Honours, this exhibit is already --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Is already in evidence, and it's in evidence as D443. The reason I'm using this specific copy is just because it's more legible than the version in evidence. And I seek to tender this specific -- this version, Your Honours. Unless Your Honours do not consider it necessary. I know it's already part of another exhibit which the Defence has tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid this has already been admitted as D443. Perhaps that is of assistance. I stand to be corrected, if I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that's correct. And the question is whether we should receive this as a separate exhibit or as an addition to 443. I think we'll receive it as a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01537.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just on the topic of meetings, sir, do you recall a meeting that took place on the 17th of May, 1999, which General Ojdanic attended and which was also attended by other members of the VJ and some representatives of the MUP, and the topic of this meeting was the security situation in Kosovo including crimes committed in Kosovo? Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise. A meeting where in whose office? I'm not sure what the type of the meeting you have in mind. At the supreme commander's or in the Supreme Command staff premises?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I was talking about a meeting in the premises of the Supreme Command staff attended by these persons. Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I don't recall a single meeting at which there were people in attendance who were outside the composition of the Army of Yugoslavia where the Supreme Command was briefed on anything. And not only the Army of Yugoslavia, but of the police as well. At the location where there were meetings of the Supreme Command staff, there was no access to anyone -- for anyone else save for those military personnel who were members of the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, I just misspoke. I meant at the supreme commander's. I didn't mean at the premises of the Supreme Command staff.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that such a meeting was held with the supreme commander. It would have entailed co-ordination and co-operation between the army and MUP. In such light it would be logistic for a meeting of that nature to be held. As for the 17th of May specifically, that is something I cannot recall as a date for such a meeting, but by the nature of the situation such meetings did, indeed, take place at the supreme commander's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay, sir, I understand. You don't recall that specific meeting. Just going back to the evening briefings very briefly, and this is the last document I want show you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could have D008-2171 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall any discussion -- while this document is being brought up, I just wanted to put a question to you -- do you recall any discussion at these evening briefings towards the end of May 1999 about the indictment that had been issued by this Tribunal against members of the Serbian leadership including General Ojdanic? Do you recall any discussion about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the indictments being discussed at any briefings about charges being brought and indictments issued. There may have been mention, though, of that possibility of indictments being issued, but I don't ever recall having heard a discussion on specific indictments which had been issued prior to such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. If we look at this page, and this is the briefings of the 28th of May, 1999. Under number 2 where Major-General Krga speaks, if we look it at the last bullet point it says: "Bringing an indictment has several purposes, one of them is, of course, stalling peace initiatives." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I put to you, sir, that this reference here we have in this minutes is in fact a reference to the indictment that was being prepared and had been issued by this Tribunal which included charges against General Ojdanic and other members of the Serbian leadership. You don't recall hearing this discussion on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The way it is formulated here, I really don't know where you draw the inference that this pertains to any ICTY indictments. These could have been any other type of indictments. It could have been proceedings held before our military courts or as part of our judiciary. I don't recall such discussions ever being held in the context of the International Tribunal in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You did say earlier, though, that you do recall there being mention of a possibility of indictments being issued, and I ask you this in the context of an indictment issued by this Tribunal. Was that discussed, the possibility of this Tribunal bringing an indictment against members of the Serbian leadership including General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I did not have such knowledge. I can't say specifically that this was discussed in such precise terms and in that context.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say it wasn't discussed in such precise terms, can I -- can we conclude that there was discussion on the topic, or are you saying something else when you say you can't recall it was discussed in such precise terms?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I try to be more precise, then I would be more inclined towards stating that it was not discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01538.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Defence will have certain questions in our redirect. Firstly, let's go back to D587. In particular, entry 248, only the B/C/S original. Zoom in, please, so that we can have a good view of item 248. D587. This is not it. Yes, I guess this is it. 248, please. Zoom in. The page on the opposite side of this one, column number 8. So the continuation of entry 248.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We would have to deal with this Vlajkovic entry. First of all, you said that this was not your signature?
