utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Secondly, who wrote Vlajkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person authorised to do so. The person in charge of the log-book. At that time it was staff sergeant, I think, the head of the sub-office Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What's his first name?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miodrag.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under 248 we have two documents. In the archive list, there's only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which means that such an error could not have happened to our chief -- or head of sub-office. I allow for the possibility that this was inserted later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How much later?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I was no longer with the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who was your successor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have happened in 2001 when there was a technical check of all archival material from 1998 and 1999. That took place in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This clarifies a lot your previous answer you gave to my learned friend. My next question has to do with D585, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please zoom in on the bottom of that page on the left-hand side. Please zoom in on the left-hand side bottom part.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the stamp you discussed with my learned friend having previously discussed it with me as well. Firstly, you said that this document, D585, and the other one, P888, I think, I don't think we need to bring it up because we have discussed it so extensively that I believe you recall all the details. In any case, my learned friend asked you who told you that this was an important document, and you said that that was your own conclusion. I'm asking you this: Given that you say that you don't know about this document and that you don't know of the other document which remained with the 3rd Army that was signed by General Lazarevic which logically speaking would have preceded this document that is in front of us, to ask you again, because I have to, give that you had the obligation to control the implementation of tasks and orders of the Chief of Supreme Command staff, do you recall given the issue raised in this document signed by General Pavkovic, that there was any contact with MUP regarding that, or were you circumvented and Mr. Gajic contacted directly? Is it possible that you didn't know about any activities undertaken following this document particularly having in mind that you say that the document was of some importance?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is addressed to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command which means that he was supposed to received it -- had to have received it. Had he received it, he would have reacted to it, which mean that is he would have written on the document itself who would have any duties regarding from the organisational units of the Supreme Command staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the counsel please repeat his question and the witness repeat his answer because the speakers are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you just pause, please. You and Mr. Djordjevic are speaking too quickly and at the same time. We have to go back to your question and then the answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat. I put the question in view of this importance of the document, is it possible that in view of the position that you had during the war, in the office of the Supreme Command staff, that you had been circumvented and not been informed about the contents of the document and had not been asked to react to the document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's practically impossible for this document not to come to the office after the Supreme Command -- the Chief of the General Staff had looked at it except relating to specific assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Except for the chief of security Gajic, I think, would you personally have had to have known about this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the methodology of the work, I would have had to forward this document for action to Gajic and not only Gajic, but to some other or organs of the command and possibly some institutions along the vertical line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you be the person who would control whether the orders, the commands of the chief of the General Staff were implemented, and would you have to report back on that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, once an assignment was implemented, Colonel Gajic or the others who would be entrusted with tasks from this document would have to report back about the implementation of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As my colleague asked you, are mistakes possible - I'm going to ask you directly - if it's possible whether this stamp was put on the document later?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry, the Defence has been carried away by the factual state and by my profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to repeat my question: As my learned friend Ms. Kravetz asked you, is it possible for mistakes to have occurred during the drafting of the archive log-book, I'm going to ask you whether it's possible, I'm directly asking you whether this stamp was put on the document later once you had left the duties of which you were in the office?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. And the complete problematics relating to these three documents would tend to indicate that. The log-book, the archives, and this document that we are looking at now. It's quite possible, because the same person had remained and worked in the office after me for some time definitely. I don't know for how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I move to my next question, I would like to see again the first page of this document, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend insisted on you allowing for the possibility that P888 is a copy of this document, namely that that possibility was a realistic one. You explained to my learned friend that that was practically impossible and illegal to say the least, and quite contrary to the rules that we had discussed yesterday. I'm asking you now, if we look on the right side of the document, it says, Copy number, and that is blank, and then if we go back to that, if there is a blank for the copy number here, is it possible then that there is P888 as a copy, this is short and sweet, and it has to do with the rules that we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could always make a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But do you need to put a number on it though? This is what I'm asking you, the copy number.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The original would bear number 1, and copy would bear number 2 if there were no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So what does that indicate in terms of P888 if it's not there, the copy number here or there?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the most simple -- the simplest explanation would be that it was not sent to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my next question has to do with these briefings. I would just like to clarify completely one story that has to do with the understanding and the use of certain terms. We spoke about the evening briefings, meetings, and you said that Mucibabic, Paskas colonels were taking minutes by hand, it was not a stenogram. And they managed to write down whatever they managed to write down. This here, as a consequence possibly of such minutes, is something that you refer to as a transcript. We understand a transcript to be what is transcribed from the audiotape or an audio recording. Would we be able to call it what my learned friend Ms. Kravetz called it handwritten minutes, and relating to the authenticity of this document, would you be able to say whether it's undoubtedly something that is authentic or perhaps can there be any doubt as to the authenticity of these minutes? Is there a possibility that they are not authentic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry for being imprecise. When I say transcript, I would mean by that what is not typed out. I did not differentiate between an audiotape and a written down notice. These minutes were taken by hand and then they were typed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let us stop here. This handwritten note, where was that written down?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This what written down in the book, log-book of minutes of the Supreme Command staff at the command staff premises during the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was this a bound book or loose-leafed book?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a bound book in hard covers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you notice if possibly a page of the book was torn out?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pages were numbered and that could also be an indicator if something like that was done. It would be noticed in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And you as the Chief of the Supreme Command office, did you ever co-operate with somebody, or did you issue anyone an assignment for those handwritten minutes to compare these briefings from the book with these ones here?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that anyone ever after you, once you left the chief's office perhaps did something like that, that they compared these two and verified them?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. Since all of that was archived by the end of the year, I'm really don't know about anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So you have no information that this was ever verified or authorised by any authorised official?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are now going to go back to document which was admitted here. This is document P101354 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at this document on the e-court. I can see in the transcript that the number is wrong. The number of the document. The document is P1534. Can we please look at this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In reference to this document, you said that as far as the MUP was concerned, actually, we saw there the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Republican Ministry of the Internal Affairs should be informed and that the person in charge of this by establishment was the chief of security Colonel Gajic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was the chief of the administration at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Administration for security?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And now, do you have information whether he co-operated with the ministry, or did he co-operate more with one of the departments within the MUP? Let me remind you, we have two departments: Public securities department and state security department. Do you have that information?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have precise information about that, but since I know Gajic, he mostly referred to co-operation with the state security department. But we did contact them in writing through the MUP chiefs office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to one of these evening briefings, my learned friend mentioned, and she just asked you whether you noticed that paragraph 2 in the minutes states that a denial should be issued regarding the refugees. Do you have any other comments on that other than you having said that yes, I see that that is written there?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understood in that briefing from what I can recall, there were some overexaggerated writing in the press about refugees from Kosovo. Since that number, according to our assessment, and I'm talking about the assessment of the Supreme Command staff, was not nearly that figure, and since a number of those refugees were directed towards Sandzak, Montenegro, and south-eastern Serbia, the information bureau was informed to issue a denial in the media and to explain what it was really about, to explain the extent, the causes, and the consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And that is your answer?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, we are going to have a small -- yes, let me check something.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the translation here, I think that that is line 1 and 2 and page 52. In the transcript it says that when you were explaining first that Gajic got in touch with members of the state security, you also say that: "Q. I would try to translate that back to you, but we had contacts with them. You are thinking of --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Command staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, that the Supreme Command staff got in touch with the MUP," and here it says, "through the main office of the MUP?"

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the cabinet, the office of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Whose office?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office of the minister of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right, and that is clear now. My learned friend mentioned several times paramilitaries, paramilitary units as a problem. I would like to ask you, you explained that there were attempts to uncover such units and if they were not resubordinated to the army or not pursuant to the positive laws of the then-state, which was called the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, such people were then disarmed, and you said that you would return them. I don't know where you returned them to, but this is not what I want to ask you. I want to ask you, as far as I'm concerned, the paramilitary unit to me means something that should be under the army but is not under the army, and the para-police forces could be, for example, the reserve compositions of the MUP, perhaps. According to me, that's not it either, so I'm asking you to give a distinction here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are there putting specific information and knowledge and a view that you have to the witness instead of asking the witness what does he mean or what is meant by a paramilitary force. You having done that, his answer now has lost much of its value, whatever it may be. Do you understand the problem? Thank you. Would you proceed as you think best.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. I completely accept your objections and the reaction by my learned friend as well as your reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question would be, what do you imply that paramilitary forces means specifically, and what would that mean exactly in our language, what should that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would mean that these are armed compositions which are outside of the systems of the command of the army which happen to find themselves there without having been sent there by the command units of the Army of Yugoslavia. This is what we considered to be paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In regard finally let me ask you about the last document that was shown to you, and that is document -- actually, it's an article in the "Politika" daily. At these briefings of the Supreme Command staff chief, was there ever any discussion about articles in newspapers or what was written in newspapers?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Command staff administration for information and morale monitored that particular area, and it was responsible for contacts with the media, with foreign journalists, domestic journalists and media. So as part of their briefings, the chief of the administration would present certain things that were noticed in the press about the writing in the press. But as for specific meetings, this was not discussed because what was written in the press was never on the Supreme Command staff agenda. Although, in certain evaluations and assessments by the information administration, there were reactions issued to some writings in the press, specifically the denial about the extent or the scale of the migration of the population, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And this would be my last question in my redirect, I'm thanking you for coming to testify. Your Honours, I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry, but I have to take you back again to the log-book we saw several times during your testimony. D588. The left page I would like to have on the screen. Only the left side of this document, please. Earlier you answered the question of the Defence counsel who was it who took the notes here and made this entry. Could you perhaps tell us who was the person? You mentioned Miodrag Jankovic. Was it the person who made these -- all these handwritten entries?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, Mr. Jankovic was the office manager of the office of the Supreme Command staff chief, and this is his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: All handwritings -- all notice on this page?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would really have to look at everything. Since he had an assistant who was also an active-duty serviceman, it is possible that this other person entered some of these document, and that his handwriting can appear here. That is to say, the handwriting of Mr. Jankovic and his assistant, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These are two different persons. Do we know the handwriting of both persons?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one appeared more frequently and, therefore, I recognise it more easily, but if I had an opportunity to look at Mr. Nikolic's handwriting, I'm not sure if I would be able to recognise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, once again, the entry under number 248, there are two different entries, as we know, both from the same person or from different persons?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is evident that different pencil was used, but as for the handwriting, I would say it belongs to one and the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And that is, as I understood you, Mr. Miodrag Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to have a look on the other document, D587, the same page, please. On this page we can see all entries in column number 5. Perhaps you can tell us, what is written down there? Just one entry after the other, what does it mean? Starting at 247.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that according how these columns are arranged, information about the received documents were entered in the order of receipt in the office. 247, the next one is 248, 249, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is written there in column number 5 under item 247? What does it mean? Read it, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Command of the 3rd Army."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now, 248, the two entries.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "SMO" stands for the Federal Ministry of Defence "- administration for defence preparations," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Why do you say "et cetera?"

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't read it because it is an illegible copy. I know the exact name of this administration, and it's not being fully entered because it's a very long name, and you couldn't put it in one column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then the next entry, the next line?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under 2 entered on the 26th of May, it reads, "Command of the 3rd Army - forward command post" or IKM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And now 249?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a poor copy, but I would say that this is a sector of RV and PVO which stands for air force and anti-aircraft defence, and it was registered as an incoming document coming from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And please continue with 250.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Supreme Command staff - sector for operations and staff affairs. It's one of the organisational units of the Supreme Command staff," which means that this was a document produced by this particular sector and was sent either to the office of the chief or for someone to act upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There are two dates, 15th and 26th of May, 1999, but without an entry in column number 5, the second date. Have you any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether somebody had intended to enter something on the 26th of May and then gave up on the idea, I cannot tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to item 251, two entries. What is written there in column number 5?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1: "Supreme Command staff, sector for education, training, and scientific publications." Under number 2: "Federal Ministry of Defence - sector for," I think it is CP which stands for civilian affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And now the next entry, 252?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Federal Ministry of Defence - Secretariat of the ministry" because that was one of the ministry units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And then the next line, 19th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recognise this acronym, primarily because this is a poor copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And number 253, 16th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is SP, which is a designation for the document produced in the office itself. So if you look in the archives under 253, you would see exactly what it contains. And this SP stands for own product, literally translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The next column is blank on item 253. There is no registration number. Do we have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that in relation to this document of ours, there were no other related documents, so this number remained only with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And now the last item 254 with four entries, four different dates.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 16th of May, the Federal Ministry of Defence, SMO - Secretariat, sent a document, and it was received under number 1. At this moment I cannot tell what the content was and probably under 2, the sector for recruitment, third administration reacted to this previous document by providing a response and probably because it deals with the same topic, it was entered under number 2. There is further correspondence related to this matter. I have lost the image on my screen. I've touched the screen, and I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There it is again.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So document number 3 is own product, something that was issued by the office, and finally number 4, "Sector for education, training, and scientific publication," which means that they also had some connection with this original document under number 1. So we have four documents under 245 [as interpreted] which all generate one from another. That is why they are related. This facilitates the tracing of documents, and the handling of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I shan't keep you very long. I just want you to help me with a small definition you gave coming to the end of your re-examination. You described the paramilitary units, and you said that they are armed compositions which are outside the system of the command of the army, which happen to find themselves there without having been sent there by the command units of the VJ. Now, can you assist us as to by whom would they have been sent?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, but I only have subsequent knowledge in that respect. Units were sent to combat zones by political parties. Those were groups of volunteers armed by political parties and were sent down there in compliance with their propaganda in order to defend the people or depend the territory. As far as I and my colleagues learned later, there were several such paramilitary formations set up by various political parties in Serbia. All of that was beyond any influence or any capability of the army to prevent that, and they did their best to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... and this particular information you would have required subsequent, not at the particular time?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. Precisely so. At a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will be pleased to know, sir, that completes the questions for you today. The Chamber would thank you for your attendance here again and for the assistance you've been able to give. You may return to your normal activities and a Court Officer will show you out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our next witness should be Mr. Dusan Mladenovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you please read aloud the affirmation which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please repeat. I'm sorry, I didn't have my headphones on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read the affirmation which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mladenovski.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Dusan Mladenovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: On the 11th of June, 1957.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: In the village of Vladimirovo, Berovo [Realtime translation read in error "Birovo"] municipality, Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, on 14th of June, 2008, did you give a written statement to investigator Ratko Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: But I would just like to correct the name of the municipality is not Birovo but rather Berovo, B-e-r-o-v-o.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So on the 14th of June, 2008, did you give a statement to investigator Ratko Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was on the 14th June or January.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, January.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Before your today's evidence, did you have an opportunity to look at this statement of yours given in January 2008?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you were to be asked the same questions, would you repeat today everything that you told Mr. Djukanovic at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I tender the statement of Dusan Mladenovski number D010-0685 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00608.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you give evidence in the Milutinovic et al. trial I think on the 21st and 22nd of April, 2008?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you repeat today everything that you said on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender the evidence of Mr. Dusan Mladenovski in the Milutinovic transcript, D010-3302 to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00609, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness carried out administrative duties in the army. He reviewed and received archive materials. He reported for duty at the archive on the 13th of July, 1999, and he is going to testify about the archiving procedure including corrections and entering of new material into the archive. He is capable of identifying incorrectly registered information that are not in compliance with standard archiving procedure, particularly written amendments that were not properly certified and authenticated. The witness is going to help us with identifying certain pieces of evidence in this case, and he is going to convey to us what he knows about what the proper archiving procedure should and would be. So this would be a short summary of the evidence to be given today by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovski, can you please tell us something about your educational background?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: I finished secondary military school of ground forces, which lasted four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is that all?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about your career?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: From 14th of July, 1975, when I finished school and started working, I was a platoon commander and I also work as a desk officer for general affairs, and I was an office manager of the mailing room. Then I was a desk officer for organisation and mobilisation, and as of the 13th of July, 1999 until the termination of my service on the 31st of December, 2006, I was the handler of archive material.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Department which covered the period up to 19 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: After 1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When were you pensioned off?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: On the 31st of December, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us specifically what your duties were in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Since the premises where the military archive was housed was relocated or actually the material was relocated from the premises that were damaged, we were scattered on different locations. For that reason, I was not able to carry out my duties. After that, the chiefs entrusted us with a task of reviewing and receiving the archives that were produced during the war operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovski, was there a rule in force, regulation, or instructions that you used in the course of your work in the archives, save for the instructions you received from the chief of the military archives or other department chiefs which is something one would suppose you did?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: There are instructions on the reception, protection, and use of archival material. Given that the material in question was rather specific, the chief of the military archives and department chiefs, before we began working on that material, carried out additional preparations. They issued separate instructions and guide-lines about how we were to review and receive the material. As for any need for clarification we may require in the course of our work, we always had the chiefs at our disposal. If there was anything in question, we could always put questions to them in order to receive further guide-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you work on the archiving the war-time material including the documents received from the Chief of Supreme Command staff and his office?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: I did not work on the archiving process itself. I worked on receiving and reviewing that material.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you work also in the process of receiving the material --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: -- when the war-time material is in question? I want to ask you about the rule per se because it is already in evidence and anyone interested may peruse it. I wanted to ask you something else. You said that per establishment there was a chief of the military archives. Next there were two department chiefs. Firstly, tell us what those departments were, and who the chiefs were by the first and last name, if you recall. That would be the first question. The second, to the best of your recollection, can you tell us what instructions did you receive concerning those documents which were not encompassed in the rule we mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: At the helm of the military archives, there was a chief. Within the archives there were two departments as well as a general affairs -- general administrative affairs department. The first department dealt with archival material dating back to 1887 until the 15th of May 1945. In that department, the material contained therein was completely processed in terms of archival science, and it was open to public. The second department contained material created after 1945, that is to say, after the 15th of May. They were in charge of that period. And I was appointed clerk for archival material in the first department, that is the department dealing with material up to 1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about during war time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Since I could no longer perform my establishment duty during that time, the chiefs decided to use all available personnel who could not perform their regular duties to assign to the process of receiving and reviewing archival material.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall any specific instructions that went beyond certain rules which were in place that you received from the chief? You did say that you received separate instructions. If you recall, can you just tell us the most important points?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: The most important point was that the material concerned required different handling. In peacetime it is handled differently. During war time, the person receiving such material upon observing a mistake would return that for correction.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: That was the situation in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, given that the material in question was voluminous, they decided that the documents should not be returned to the author for correction, but they provided us some guide-lines that we were supposed to follow. And I apologise for not having answered the second part of the question. The chief of the first department at the time was Colonel Nikola Bibic and the chief of the second department was Lieutenant-Colonel Stanislav Krstic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about the chief of the military archives?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Colonel Velimir Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall any other instructions, for example, those dealing with the contents of those documents?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: If I need to explain in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps it will be best to do it using a document, but I can also just simply tell you that. The instructions were received was for us to control the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, 6th, and 7th column. They excluded the 3rd column. The chief of the military archives put particular stress on the importance of us not reading the documents even to the extent that we would need to enter a brief remark, but not to read it at all, he insisted on that with the department chiefs, to caution us not to do that. Among other things one of the reasons was probably that we should not waste our time reading through the documents in order to complete the job ASAP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As part of your work were there any other persons present engaged on the same task?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, there were between 10 and 12 of us concerning receiving and reviewing the material. When you asked me a moment ago about the archives of the Supreme Command staff, if you went through all of the material, you would probably come across different names of people who were in charge of receiving and reviewing documents, including myself. I don't know if I'm make myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Concerning the corrections you were supposed to make, firstly, were there any deviations or departures from the rule that was in force in terms of handling archival material or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: If one would consider a departure what I have already mentioned, then it was a different procedure. We no longer returned documents to the authors for correction. We made them ourselves. And as for anything that may have been unclear, the chiefs were there to provide instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So instead of returning documents to the sender, you were authorised to make corrections following the procedure given to you by the chief?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: While on the topic of corrections, please describe what you did precisely, from the moment when you receive an archive list with new documents, let's start with that.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: A person who would bring in documents in bulk would usually bring documents in bundles, and we probably always went by archival unit based on the archive list. For example, entry number 1, we would take the documents belonging to that particular archival unit in order to check whether the number of documents tallies, the number of sheets, and if there was anything else. For example, to see whether it was a photocopy or another document attached to the original. And we were supposed to make corrections that were supposed to be visible. We followed the bookkeeping method, meaning that we would simply cross out an incorrect digit and write by hand the correct number of documents or sheets. These were columns 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's stop here. In order to make it clear to all those who are following, we would perhaps need to see documents from a binder we have prepared for the witness. I would kindly ask the usher to assist us in that. We have hard copies in that binder that the witness can peruse. Could we please have D584 on the screen. Only the Serbian version, please, because we have been seeing it so frequently in the course of the past few days. Could we please zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder, Mr. Mladenovski, that is number 1. Please go on with your explanation. This is the archive list that we are discussing?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Briefly only, do you recognise this document as the document you drafted as opposed to the documents of other people who worked alongside you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, this is my list. You can see on page 8 that I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We'll discuss that later. We were still with the corrections you made and how you entered them. Let us zoom in on the table part alone where the columns are. And then we can go by numbers. What is the blue patch here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The white patch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, I have no idea why this was covered, and by whom, I have no explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's start with 1 and go down to 6. Let's go by columns rather.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Before that, let me tell you this, this is the archive list. This was a template form for the hand-over of archival materials and documents. Archival unit 1, entry 1 in column 1, then binder 2 is in column 2. In column 4 we have the log-book number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about column 3?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: I was about to get there. So in the fourth column we have 134-1,2. Two documents and three sheets. This means that the person handing over the documents wrote that there were only two sheets. When I checked, I established that there were three. Most of the mistakes occurred with the number of sheets because the sender usually did not count them carefully. If there were any remarks or cover pages when we specifically speak of the Chief of Supreme Command staff, their documents always had a cover page and in such cases the sender usually disregarded that. And at the beginning of, say, a plan or some such document, they merely forgot to count that page because it only contained a title. However, according to archival science, even if there's a single letter on a sheet of paper, it is a document. For that reason we needed to make the corrections. I don't know if I'm making myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will resume after the break although we are already late for that break. I just wanted to round off this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic. Could the Chamber point out that there is no value in us using time unnecessarily. The witness's statement deals with quite a bit of the detail of the work that he did and what he did with this exhibit. Similarly his evidence in the previous trial canvassed some of this again. We just don't have the time in this case to receive his statement and his transcript and then go over all his evidence again in detail. So if you could bear that in mind during the break to see how you could bring him to just the most essential points that are additional to those that are in his statement and his transcript. Thank you. We adjourn now and we resume just after 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the witness enters, I wanted to draw your attention to D609, the transcript, given that a significant portion of it was given in private session, I would kindly ask that it be admitted under seal. Also, we have the redacted version. It is D011-2810. And I would like to have that admitted as well. So D609 admitted under seal. We have already admitted that, and I apologise for not having directed your attention to that fact. And the second one is D011-2810. It is the redacted version, and I seek to tender that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. D'Ascoli?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Just to clarify because I don't remember the testimony of Mr. Mladenovski entirely -- mostly in private session during the MOS trial. I was looking at my version of the transcript and I have it from page 25769, I don't have the current court page, until two pages late, and that's all I have in private session, so if maybe my learned counsel can verify that, probably there's no need to have one version under seal and the other with redaction, or -- it was just a suggestion because I don't remember that mainly in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We won't delay the witness now, we'll look at that and deal with it at another time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, respecting what you said just before the break, I will strive to conclude my redirect -- my direct examination as soon as possible, especially bearing in mind that it is Friday afternoon and that the witness should go home since he awaited his testimony for a number of days. Another option is since the courtroom is free in the afternoon, we may ask for some additional time to conclude the witness today. I also forgot to say that Ms. Aapio an intern of ours is with us here today. I will continue with my direct examination. Could we please go back to D584 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are not in a position to continue after 1.45, so if we can finish by then it will be wonderful.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have D584 and D583 placed next to each other. The B/C/S versions. D584 and 583.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see the transcript had me saying 1450 hours. That's not so. It's 1.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I would rather like that you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I won't delay you further, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D584 and D583. One next to each other. I think this is one in the same version. D584 and D583. That's it. Much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovski, is this the same document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: It is, however, the one on the left has column number 3 covered, pasted over. And on the left document, I don't see the stamp in the upper right-hand corner, whereas the one on the right does.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'll stop you right there. We see a part of the form on the right-hand side where the figure of 21606 is. What is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: As I said, this is a standard template when there is any hand-over of archival material and documents. In the upper right-hand side corner we have the inventory number containing the inventory number of the archive list in question. Next is the date when the material was received and reviewed. Next we have a total of documents and of sheets. This is standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who inserts figures there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: It is done after having received the documents. We have the date of the 24th September. I put in the number of sheets. As for the inventory number, it was entered by the person who was in charge of filing it following our review.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question. The number of documents and sheets, is it including the corrections or without?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: The number of documents and number of sheets, I believe you originally said pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: That is the number with the corrections entered in columns 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the last page of both documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since we have it on the screen now, can you tell us who made the annotations, the handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: The bottom left corner list compiled by warrant officer and the right bottom corner, colonel who was the chief. He was chief of office of the Supreme Command. As for the handwritten notes in the last column, we have my signature there and the note says: "Received and reviewed by Mr. Mladenovski."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What was the rule concerning corrections? You said you followed the bookkeeping method of crossing out?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, and then we would enter the correct number above the incorrect one, unless the previous number was at the very top of the box when you can't fit your correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to item 82, please. You could do it on the right-hand side document, page 2. Please zoom in so that we have entry 82 alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at that. Your comment, first of all, is this your correction?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: This is an archival unit line 82, and just like I told the investigator en route in the statement and confirmed in the previous transcript and I'm confirming now that I was not the one who made this correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And you're claiming this on what basis?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: First of all, on the basis of the instructions of my chiefs on how to make corrections. Had I made this correction, if we look at this box 5 and 6, there is enough space for the numbers to be written above the line, and evidently, they were written here below. That's one thing that would seem to prove my assertion. And secondly, if you look at the entire list from first to last page, none of the boxes was corrected with the number below, only that archival unit with the number 82.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And did you later check the subtotal that you spoke about? We saw the first page of the form and all of them and we saw the number of the pages. Does that correspond?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: I checked that when I was giving my statement to the investigator Ratko Djukanovic, and that was when we established that without this correction in the archive unit number 82, without that correction there taking into account all the other corrections, the number of the documents does tally and comes to 277, the number of pages tallies and is 735.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Including this correction?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: With this correction, then you would have 278 documents or 737 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have an idea who could have made this correction other than you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Well, let me first tell you that the correction could have happened after the 24th of September, 1999, after I signed the list. So from the 25th of September, 1999 on until the time this document was photocopied. I don't have any idea who could have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That will be enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we place D588 and D587 Serbian version next to each other, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And what is this about?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: I see here the log-book or a photocopy of the log-book of the cabinet of the Supreme Command staff chief from 1991 [as interpreted]. We can see that this is book 4 -- book 1 and starts from the number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we please look at the entry 248 in this log-book. Can we look at both the documents in the second document I think this box would be on page 7, on the left-hand side. And your comment, please, is this more or less the same thing?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: I see here, well, I apologise. I see the number 248-1, that it was logged in on the 15th of May, 1999, and as far as I can see, the federal defence ministry administration for, it doesn't matter, then 248-2 on the 26th of May, 1999, this was sent from the command of the 3rd Army forward command post 872-94/1-2. I could possibly give you my comment because in the course of my career, I did perform some log keeping duties. I don't know how much that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is not the question. My question relates to this, did you have the opportunity so have this log-book in your hands in preparation for testimony here?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: I did, during my previous testimony, it was presented to me. I personally did not -- I don't know, perhaps it was in some archive list that perhaps I received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And can you comment here about this entry or not? Can you just tell me that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: I've told you, I can just do it on the basis of my experience. Because I did those kinds of assignments during my career, so there is no logic there in the sense of linking one document to the other because usually you would link together the same topics if something referred to the same topics. Evidently here, I don't know, as I say, we did not. The chief forbade us strictly to read texts so the administration for preparation and the 3rd Army Command, I don't know whether there would be something in common there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I would like to thank the witness for this, for coming today. I would like to complete my examination-in-chief. And I would like to tender page 2574 -- or transcript pages which were in the private session 25767 to 25769. And that is why we said we would like to keep this under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic, we'll look at the question of private session and seal later. We will try and deal with the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but those pages are in private session so there is no problem about that. I just understood that he wanted the whole transcript done. It was a different issue, sorry, I was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I'll try to be quick, Mr. Mladenovski, so that we can finish today.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: You have already -- can we call on the screen can we call back the exhibit, the archive list D584, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And you have already explained in your statement also is pretty much detailed all the procedure and your duties in this archive procedure so I won't go into that, but if we -- I'm waiting for the document to be on the screen. If you go to the last page of this document, as you said we see the signature at the bottom of the last page of warrant officer Miodrag Jankovic who was supposedly the person who prepared the list, is that correct, from the office of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. And you received this list as compiled by this warrant officer. Your duty, as we said, was to verify the accuracy and we learned that you corrected many mistake on the list. I was going through this list just to have a look at the mistakes, and I could notice that we have over, more or less over 60 mistakes in this list. So would it be fair to say, Mr. Mladenovski, that this list you received wasn't a perfect example of accuracy; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Well, you could say that it's not an example of accuracy or correctness, but there were some archival lists that were 100 per cent accurate. And unfortunately, there were some with many more errors, but like I said, in the instructions issued to us by the chiefs and in order not to waste time and in order to complete that job, they suggested that we carry out the error -- the corrections --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Of course. We heard about that. May I stop you there so that we can proceed quickly. You said that of course there were lists with zero errors but there were also lists with many errors, and my point was that this list that we are discussing it was an example of inaccuracy and presented many errors. That was my point. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I suppose that during your job at the archives between the 13th of July, 1999 and 2001, you had to inspect and check many of these archive lists, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Would you be able to give us an approximate number of, for example, how many lists you corrected in the first two months you worked there meaning July until September 1999? Just an approximate number. Was it like hundreds, thousands, hundreds of thousands?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I have no idea, but the person who did take care of these -- this information afterwards would probably have the precise data. I don't have the precise data. We did not keep records of who did how much.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I understand that. I was just asking whether you went over many of these lists in terms of numbers in those first months or you corrected just a few of these archive lists received from the, for example, the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: I really cannot remember, please believe me.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No problem. Your work on this list and in particular on the one that we have on the screen, in any case, dates back to more than ten years ago by now; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: More than ten years, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that you can't remember specifically this list that we are looking at in the sense that you can't have a specific memory about this list, but you recognise that you dealt with it because you've seen it or it's on the last page of it indicating that you were the clerk, the officer who was assigned to review and correct this list?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Not only the signature but when looking at the numbers also that I corrected that would be on the basis of that as well. And it's also in the list. You can see other handwritings, and I made the entries myself by hand. This is how I can tell, by the handwriting and the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. So you said that you recognise all the corrections made in this list with the exception of the archive unit 82; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And you said you recognise those corrections -- you don't recognise also the correction at the archive unit 82 because the numbers were written below rather than above the new digits that were entered because they were not according to the procedure?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Not just the fact that they were written below, but also by looking at my numbers, I don't write numbers in that way. If you look at this other list, you can probably see that the numbers are different.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we then go at page 3. We can just keep the B/C/S version. I don't need the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If we go at page 3 of the original archive list, and for example, we have a look at the archive unit number 29. The correction that you entered, this digit the number 2, was that entered by you; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And if we scroll up a bit and we look also at the archive unit number 21, also this other number 2 was written by you; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Would you then agree that at least on the face of them, these two number 2s, they look slightly different? They don't look exactly the same way?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: They look different but that would again depend on the speed of writing and whatnot. Maybe perhaps if one were not in a rush, the numbers would be written slightly differently, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. So you would concede that your way of writing the number 2 would differ depending on, of course, the way you were writing and in the first case the archive unit 21 we see that there's a straight termination of the 2 while at archive unit number 21 we see there is a more curved termination of the 2? Of course, I'm not like a handwriting expert like yourself, you're not too, but I was just asking whether you agree with this difference which is pretty evident, and you said you did, so thanks for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we move to page 5 of the archive list.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Also here, sir, would you agree that for example, the way the number 2s are written in the different corrections we see, they don't look always the same, and I'm talking about line 51 and then compare with line 54 or 56. Doesn't this confirm what you said, depending on the speed of writing numbers could end up being written differently?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Correct. In 54, it's slightly different. But as I'm saying, this is at the point of time that it was written.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I was just asking about that, thank you. Now, if we go to the problematic archive unit number 82. This is at page 7, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Wouldn't you agree that, for example, the way the number 2 is written in column 5 of archive unit 82 resembles the way the number 2 is written in archive unit number 21, for example -- 29, the one that we saw at page 3 of the archive?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: I would agree that it is somewhat alike, but I think this is really evident, this top part where the 2 is written. You are just looking at the bottom part of the actual number. I think that -- there is a difference there. If you permit me to tell you as far as my previous testimony is concerned, this would be the final testimony in Belgrade. I did submit my handwriting to a handwriting expert attorney Ackerman asked that and I said that yes, I agreed to provide a sample of my handwriting, and I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sure, but it's not the case in this situation, so thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Excuse me, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No, no need to apologise. I was just interested in whether you would immediately recognise that the way you are writing certain numbers and the way you've written certain numbers, for example the number 2, differs on the different entries and on the different digits that we have on this archive list, that was all I was asking. Thank you, sir. Let's move on so that we can finish. I have some few questions about the procedure. I understand that you said that after you concluded your check, you would hand the bundle with the archive list to the archivist who would insert the inventory number on top. Could you please tell me how the process would continue after you checked the folder and handed everything to the archivist? Are you aware of how the procedure would continue?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: I am going to tell you the person who would receive the bundles back from us, that would be the archives person who was in charge of allocating the inventory numbers and registering the other information from that particular bundle. That is something that I am familiar with. As for what happened after that, there would be some records of that, but I don't know what would happen to that bundle later. The person was obliged to check that --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. That's what I was interested in. My question is: Do you know if someone else checked the archive list after you or if a supervisor, if someone else would go again over it or whether you were the last person in the process to check the data in the archive list and together with the relative documents? Were you the last person or someone else would run a further check after you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, in looking it over and checking for the signature, I was the last person and then after that we would hand it over to the person who would be in charge of recording it and processing it further, and then the chiefs would check that person in turn. Actually, I don't know whether they were responsible for that or somebody else. We were in one set of premises, she worked in a different office, so I don't know what happened with the bundle after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. And in any case, corrections to the archive list would be only authorised persons working in the archive would be able to make corrections to these archive lists, I take it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. I should clarify something else about -- you mentioned copies of these archive lists that were made, and you said that generally three copies were produced of these archives lists. Could you tell us at which moment in time these copies were produced?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: I don't know if I mentioned copies here or photocopies of archive lists in my testimony today. In my previous testimony I did explain in detail that archival lists are made in three or four copies generally of which the original list accompanies the original documents with the bundle. One of them would go to the military archives in order to write up the contents, and the third would be returned to the copy that -- to the office that provided the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last thing he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: The interpreter asked if you can repeat your answer, but maybe I will go through it again so that it is clearer. Before that I just wanted to clarify something that you were saying before. I had asked you about whether you were the last person or not in the process because you said that in the Milutinovic testimony, this is page 33 of the transcript in e-court, you said that when the bundles were finished, they were dealt with further and there would be a person who would check everything probably. I'm quoting from a response that you gave during your testimony. So that's why I ask you whether you were aware of being the last person or not in the process. You said that, yes, you were the last one checking the archive list. But would you agree that, would it be fair to say that someone else given than you are not completely aware of this, would it be fair to say that someone else could made additional corrections after you completed your work and you hand it in?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Well, I can explain that now. The person to whom we handed it over to who did all the logging in probably did go over that again. If they found any irregularities, they would return the list to the person who signed it, the person who had previously gone over it. So there were such cases when they noticed that something was not done, but then they would immediately return it back to the person who worked on it. And then the corrections -- the list with the corrections would be sent to that person again.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: This last person you said, in this case it would be you who signed the list, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Specifically, had I made a mistake in this list, it would have been returned to me. Not just this list, but I recall that no list was ever returned to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks for the clarification. If we could go back to the issue of the copies. I was just interested in understanding whether basically you were filling in three identical originals of the same archive list meaning that you had to put, to insert your corrections on these three copies that you received, or whether this was produced later after you had finished the checking on the archive list? Could you help me with that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: All three copies of the archives list we had to correct personally. When we would finish the first copy, we would correct the second copy, then we would correct the third copy, and then we would hand them over to the person for further processing.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for that clarification. Basically you would produce let's say, three originals at the same time, each mirroring the same corrections that you made of the document. Okay. Do you know given that you said that one of these copies would be returned to the originating unit was sent the initial archive list, do you know when this copy would be sent back to the unit, at which moment in time after you ended as a final one?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know that because this was done by the person whose job this was, so I don't know when this would be returned to the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. You don't know whether it was in a matter of a week, two weeks, or a month, or longer? You don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. No problem. Sir, I understand that these three copies of course were identical as made at the same time. So if someone else would have make a correction in those copies at a later stage after you had finished checking those, they would be obliged to make a correction on all three copies; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So that all copies would reflect exactly the same corrections. What if we also seen that these copies would be then separated in the sense that for example, one would be kept in the vault, the other one would be used for consultation, and the third one would be returned to the originating unit. Wouldn't it be fair to say that if someone had made a correction or had altered the record in one of these copy at a later stage, to do a fine job, that he or she would have had to make the same correction on all three copies in order for them to mirror the content on each other, to look identical as they should be?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. And considering -- I think you testified in Milutinovic that just for -- just from the face of it, you are not able to say whether the copies that we have here on the screen is which of the three copies this archive list is, are you able to say that, if it is the original kept in the vault or the one used for consultation purposes, or the one returned to the unit? Would you be able to say that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Based on this list, I wouldn't be able to tell which particular copy of that list is, whether that's the one that accompanied the material, whether that's the one that was kept by the military archive as information piece or whether it was the copy intended for the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, as a former VJ officer, would you have access to the VJ archives, would you have the possibility of going there and checking the copies that are kept there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: I have to correct you. I was a non-commissioned officer. Ex-non-commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: But you worked -- thanks for the correction. You worked at the archives, the VJ archives?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, as a non-commissioned officer. Not an officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sure. Sir, I was just wondering whether before your previous testimony in the Milutinovic case or before your testimony in this case considering the issue at hand, whether you went to the VJ archive office and you checked whether the copies kept there had this correction and whether, for example, both copies that you could access had this correction, did you have the chance of checking that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
utterances.text: I did not have any opportunity, and I wouldn't have liked to check that either. If any checks are necessary, there are authorised personnel who should do that. It was not my place to do the checking.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: But would you agree that would have been something to help clarifying the issues, to see whether we had -- we still have three identical copies or whether if the correction was entered at a later stage, that was done in an appropriate way just on one of those? Would that probably help clarifying the matter?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI
